speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the recent conference of business leaders which was held under the auspices of the Prices and Incomes Commission has been heralded by the government as a conference on price stability. We in this party, and many other people in this country, believe that is a misnomer. It should more correctly have been called a conference on profit maintenance, because according to the communique and everything else we have heard, this was not a conference on rolling back the cost of living to lower levels or ensuring that it will not go up. According to the communique, the business leaders agreed they would reduce the number and size of price increases they would normally have made in 1970, but they made no effort to say they would not make price increases. They said they would help in contributing to a broad program of restraint, on certain conditions. I quote from the communique:
-they emphasize that an indispensable requirement for the control of inflation is a comparable measure of restraint by wage and salary earners, by governments at all levels and indeed by everyone.
In other words, to put it in plain, simple English, they will not make as big profit increases this year as they normally would have done, provided everyone else does exactly the same in restraining any increases that

DEBATES	February 12, 1970
they might be seeking. If that is worth heralding with loud hosannas, I don't think the people of this country are going to believe it. It amounts to very little. Even this they hedged about when they said "if called upon to do so". We have not heard any loud and clear calls going out from the government asking them to do so. We do not believe this amounts to anything very real at this stage. What the people attending the conference said was that if everybody else in the country will restrain themselves, they will agree to make less profit than they would have expected to make in the normal course of events.
This afternoon the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs	(Mr. Basford)
expressed surprise. He said that we in this party had long been demanding the line of income and price restraint that we are now getting. He was surprised that we were now heaping scorn on it. I wish to again point out the difference between what we in this party have been seeking and what we have got. We have always said that voluntary restraint and moral suasion will not work, that there must be a complete, over-all income policy and not one for just one section of the population. We have on our side in this issue the Economic Council of Canada. The council has said that wherever moral suasion guidelines have been tried, they have failed. They have warned that this policy will not work in this country. I do not see why the government has the Economic Council to advise it and then flies in the face of its advice.
We in this party have always said that there must be a prices review board. Manufacturers and other business concerns intending to make price increases would have to justify them before this board. But what we are told in the communique from the Prices and Incomes Commission is that businesses have agreed to a formula by which there is no necessity for them to advise the government before a price increase is made, but that there may be a possible review after the increase. That is not what we have been asking for, Mr. Speaker. We want to see a prices review board with teeth in it, which would ensure that price increases were justified before they were made.
We have over and over again said that these reviews should be made in public so that the public would know what was going on. Instead of that, this communique states that the businesses have agreed to having these reviews made in secret. We believe, and
February 12, 1970

have stated many times, that where the taxpayers of this country have paid their money into government coffers for the use of government services, the government has no business fencing those services off from the public and carrying on their operations in secrecy.
[DOT] (8:50 p.m.)
This simply means that the government does not trust the public, that the government wants to do things which the public will not approve. The government adopts a "take it or leave it" attitude by presenting the public with a fait accompli. These are the points on which we take quite a different approach to that of the Prices and Incomes Commission.
In the fourth place, we have always said that all forms of income must be included in a prices and incomes policy. Instead, the government adopts a piecemeal approach by proposing to deal with business and labour as though they were the only sectors of the community. The previous speaker but one, and others, could hardly restrain themselves in their desire to get at the throat of organized labour. They have misquoted organized labour over and over again, not only in this debate but on other occasions. I should like to put on the record the position of organized labour as presented by the Commonwealth Press Association in Ottawa on October 15 last:
Before labour will agree to any wage freeze it must be shown that the federal prices and incomes commission can halt rising prices, says Donald Macdonald, president of the Canadian Labour Congress-
"We've prepared to sit down at any time, with any group, agency, or individual and seriously discuss an incomes policy.
"But by an incomes policy we mean that all forms of incomes would have to be considered," he said.
These would include prices, profits, salaries, professional fees, rents, wages, interest rates and all other forms of income. I say, please, let this be the last time hon. members opposite are so anxious to go gunning for labour that they say wrong things about what labour has said. Organized labour has said it is willing to sit down and discuss an incomes policy, provided all forms of income are included in that discussion. But it is not prepared to be the whipping-boy of the government so that attacks can be made on wage increases gained by organized labour. Other sections of the community have secured far larger increases.
Fifth, we have always said that the government's piecemeal approach would not work, and we say so again. What does inflation
Control of Inflation and Unemployment mean in the lives of the majority of Canadians? We have been given what was described as the classic definition of inflation, but in the lives of the majority of ordinary Canadians inflation simply means that the cost of living is rising faster than their income to meet it. In far too many cases this condition is compounded by the utter disaster of unemployment which overtakes families.
We have been told in the past that in periods like this we have to choose between a rising level of unemployment and a rising cost of living. Under the gentle ministrations of this government we no longer have that choice: we have both conditions. We have a 6.1 per cent rise in unemployment, the highest level for two years, and the cost of living has been climbing at an accelerating rate for the past three years. In 1967 it climbed by 3.6 per cent; in 1968 it climbed by 4 per cent; in 1969 it climbed by 4.5 per cent; and it is still rising in 1970. Let me point out that during this period the government and its very similar predecessor government have been at the helm. Who are the victims of this inflation? They are the old, the ill, the people on low incomes and, yes, the low-paid employed.
Hon. members opposite have been telling us about the high fringe benefits received by some members of organized labour. I wonder whether they realize that the average gross income of workers in manufacturing industries in Canada, as of November, 1969, was only $5,723. I suggest that unless the income of hon. members opposite is comparable to $5,723, it ill behooves them to heave rocks at people who receive the fringe benefits they describe. No matter how many fringe benefits they receive, it would take between now and the millenium for them to come anywhere near in sight of the type of income enjoyed by many people in this country, those who have been complaining about inflation yet whom inflation does not hurt.
What is the position of our farmers today? They have unsold wheat on their hands. Even for what they can sell, cereal crop prices have dropped between 15 and 20 per cent during the last two years. While they are unable to sell their wheat, and the wheat that they can sell has dropped in price, the interest rates they have to pay have risen from 6 per cent to 9 and 10 per cent. The prices they have to pay for farm machinery have also risen steadily over the same period.
What has the government done to meet inflation at this time? Inflation did not begin yesterday, or the day before the Prices and
February 12, 1970
3550	COMMONS
Control of Inflation and Unemployment Incomes Commission held its conference of big business leaders. Let me tell the House a few of the things the government has done to beat inflation. They talked about voluntary wage and price restraints, but they did nothing when the Steel Company of Canada and other steel companies raised the price of steel by more than 20 per cent. The government was silent when International Nickel Company raised the price of nickel by 24 per cent. In fact, the government refused the demand of the United Steelworkers of America for a public investigation of these price increases.
Having established the automobile trade pact, the government still permits the automobile manufacturers of Canada to charge the Canadian automobile purchaser more than $200 per car over the U.S. price, even though the U.S. price includes additional shipping charges. At the same time, they handed a present of forgiveness to car manufacturers to the tune of $80 million worth of customs duties that the manufacturers should have paid. The new Transportation Act has given the railways greater freedom to increase freight rates, which have risen substantially. The banks have been freed of any restrictions and can now charge any interest rate they see fit. The sky is no longer the limit because interest rates have soared beyond the sky and into the stratosphere.
The government has also raised interest rates under the National Housing Act. Today's mortgage rates run from 9 to 12 per cent, a crushing burden on any worker who wishes to purchase a home. The government has taken no action to stop land speculators. Land costs in most metropolitan cities have risen over 100 per cent during the last decade. The cost of home ownership is beyond the reach of most hourly paid workers.
This is the record of the government up to this point in its fight against inflation in this country. Do you wonder, Mr. Speaker, that Canadians from coast to coast are sceptical about this gathering of senior business personnel who, in order to join in the fight against inflation, are willing to take a little less in the way of profit than they would had they not bowed moral suasion and restricted themselves? This is not fighting inflation. This is tokenism, and tokenism of the most revolting character in the eyes of the ordinary, decent-minded Canadian.
What are the proposals that the government should lay before the provinces next week? First of all, we say there is a need for
[Mrs. Maclnnis.l

a comprehensive prices and incomes policy, and that all sectors of the population should be represented. Has the government invited the people who are suffering from inflation to any conference to discuss what can be done to solve their problems? Not on your life! The only people who have been invited to conferences are those who suffer much less from inflation than the groups to which I have referred.
[DOT] (9:00 p.m.)
As I said earlier, forms of income should be considered in making prices and incomes policy. There has been objection to having control, selective or otherwise. Objections to controls come from the type of people and groups who say we are suffering from inflation. But these people are not concerned about individuals who suffer from inflation and who have seen the cost of living go up, up and up to the point where they are not able to live an ordinary and decent life.
In my city of Vancouver, during the Christmas recess I heard a welfare organization making representations to the city council. They asserted that the social welfare allowances were still at the level they were in May of 1965, while the cost of living had spiralled tremendously since that time. How can these people live? Injustice should not be frozen. Restraints should be placed on the increase in the cost of living. The 2 per cent ceiling on old age pensions must be replaced by an escalator clause. Why should old age pensioners be placed in a worsening position as a result of the cost of living today?
My colleague the hon. member for Regina East (Mr. Burton) pointed out, as far as he was able during the brief time at his disposal, what I want to mention very briefly at this time. We are not saying that these other forms of social benefit, including a guaranteed income, can be accomplished without an extension of the economic base. We have for years been urging that a Canada Development Corporation should co-ordinate and develop general economic policy in this country.
A few years ago the government was liber-ally-enough minded to believe that we might successfully introduce a policy of this kind. They talked about the establishment of a Canada Development Corporation for developing sources of income and revenue. But now the government says no more about establishing this agency. There are many things we could reduce in government spend-
February 12. 1970	COMMONS
ing. I cannot help remembering the expenditures made recently by this government, which were far from necessary. I cannot forget the Prime Minister's entourage of 17 people, at a cost of $306,165. When the former Prime Minister, Mr. Pearson, was in office he got by with seven people at an expenditure of just about half that amount, a total of $128,659. The Prime Minister before him, Mr. Diefenbaker, had three executive assistants, at a cost of less than $50,000.
If it is important that we curtail expenditures, we should begin here. The place to start restraints is right here in government. This has not taken place. As a matter of fact, if there had been restraint in this and other quarters we would not have had to spend $7 million on Information Canada this year, the agency for managing government propaganda so that the government will not receive all the lumps it would otherwise get, and deserves.
I have one more minute, Mr. Speaker. I have been watching the clock very carefully.
I feel these things should be said. The establishment of voluntary price restraints is not the way to go about solving this problem. We feel the minister should make an effort to place restrictions by law in the proper areas. We need legislation to control the cost of living, as we need it to control traffic, garbage collection and any other sectors of our living where the public needs service and protection.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I will take only about ten minutes because a number of hon. members wish to get their points across. Having listened to previous speakers across the way take part in the debate since early this afternoon, there is only one thing with which I have been impressed; that is, the insincerity of their remarks. I listened to the hon. member for Etobicoke (Mr. Gillespie) and to the remarks of the Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Regional Economic Expansion (Mr. O'Connell), and I cannot understand how hon. members can stand in the House and make remarks about the employment situation with such conviction.
There is only one conclusion that I can draw, that is, that the quicker we allow television into the House to expose the hypocrisy which takes place here, the better off the Canadian nation will be and the more respect will be shown by members of this House for the electors in this nation.
I should like to speak for a minute about my reaction to the remarks of the Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Regional Economic Expansion. If I only say this, I will be satisfied that I have made a contribution to this debate. He spoke about the great programs under the Department of Regional Economic Expansion which will create employment in Canada. For example, he indicated that we should not worry too much about unemployment because it has remained at the same level. I rise to lend my support to the motion condemning the government policies which have deliberately created unemployment up to a crisis level, thus placing the country in danger of a recession, and which have failed to stop the rapid and continuing increase in the cost of living. This House therefore calls for the immediate implementation of full employment measures and a commitment to a comprehensive prices and incomes policy.
In Saskatchewan today we are faced with the most serious economic situation we have been confronted with since the hungry thirties; I would not be exaggerating if I said, in our history. Not only have we a most serious and depressed situation in our agricultural industry, but for the first time in many years we have one of the highest rates of unemployment of any region of Canada. At one time, happily, we were rated as one of the "have" provinces but now, thanks to the policies or lack of policies of the federal government, we have again slipped back to the embarrassing category of a "have not" area of Canada.
Unemployment in the agricultural sector of the Saskatchewan economy has greatly increased as a result of the Liberal government's apparent policy of supporting the principle of providing cheaper food for Canadians at the expense of the producer. During the past year and more recently, another cause of unemployment in the prairie region has come to light. I am referring to the proposal of Canadian Na'ional Railways to implement their master agency plan all the way from the Lakehead to the Alberta boundary. This concept, developed through technological advances in recent years, is designed to concentrate the various services usually available in hundreds of stations along the CNR lines over past years into a few large urban centres, and is slated to become effective on April 1, 1970.
For the sake of the record I would like to list a number of the services that our citizens have had available to them over the years and are now to be denied. They include rail

None of us wants to close his eyes to the advantages of technological advances in our society, but coupled with this goes the responsibilities of those in authority to see that human suffering is prevented and that sociological upheavals do not take place.
A few years ago we spent many days in this House and in committee developing the new transport act, and we established a new body called the Canadian Transport Commission headed by the often referred to czar of transport, Hon. Jack Pickersgill. During those debates and deliberations we were led to believe and to hope that we had reached a sense of rationalization in all matters related to transportation. But what do we find today, particularly in western Canada which is a captive market? We find service cut-back, we find highly increased freight rates, we find many applications for rail line abandonment, and now last but not least, this master agency plan set out by a government-owned company to greatly reduce service. Mr. Speaker, the opposition motion put forward by the New Democratic party and now under study strikes me as basically ill-founded, especially because of the exaggerations it contains.
On the one hand, the government is accused of having deliberately caused economic ills such as unemployment, recession and inflation-as if a government could want such things to happen-and, on the other hand, it calls for the adoption of measures guaranteering full employement, and the application of a comprehensive prices and incomes policy.
To my mind, the motion does not make much sense, and once again, as always, we see that it is extremely easy to accuse, to criticize, and to request instant remedies to all evils, but much more difficult to suggest concrete, realist, practical and efficient steps, for instance, to check inflation, reduce unemployment and keep industrial production from decreasing.
The speeches made today by the members of the opposition contained no solution capable of solving the present economic problem which, besides, is not the monopoly of Canada, but exists as well in all industrialized countries, at least in the free world.
Canada is now faced with a number of economic problems but they are not as serious as in some other countries. The provincial governments could follow the example of the federal government and meet its suggestion by restricting their expenditures and by wholeheartedly contributing to the war against inflation. Were the big companies and other bodies also willing to co-operate, I am sure that the economic situation would improve and that confidence would be restored for, basically, our economy is sound.
We can rely on large natural resources and if we can manage to go on selling our products at competitive prices, Canada will go on expanding just as it has for the past few years, under the Liberal leadership.
Indeed, for the past seven or eight years, we have witnessed progress unprecedented in 21701-15
Proceedings on Adjournment Motion our history. During that period, Canada has demonstrated that it had grown into an industrial power. It has become one of the greatest trading nations of the world.
In the field of exports, for instance, our performance has been astonishing. From $5.2 billion in 1959 our exports have increased every year to $14.5 in 1969. This means an increase of 180 per cent over a 10-year period. If we want to get an idea of the progress made, we simply have to remember that our exports increased by 30 per cent only in the '50's which were considered quite good years.
This is due mainly to the action of this government. I will mention, for instance, the auto pact with the United States which led to better co-operation between the government and the industries, and to a better promotion of the finished products. An outstanding achievement in 1969 was the legislation introduced by the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce (Mr. Pepin) which led to the setting up of the Exports Corporation which provides new services for the promotion of exports.
To keep our markets, we have to remain competitive with other countries and curb inflation which remains at the present time the main problem facing Canada. The constant rise of consumer prices has not left unconcerned the federal government which is conscious of its role and its responsibility in that respect. It particularly looked after those on a fixed income as, for instance, those getting a pension or retirement benefits.

My concern in raising the matter of the Arrow this evening is that what happened, happened not only in one part of the country but could happen in another part of Canada. For example, if the Arrow had gone aground on the shoals on the west side of the entrance to Halifax harbour, that port would have been tied up for months and possibly years. The same could have happened in Saint John, or the St. Lawrence River, for that matter. We are met with a very serious situation and I think that three points particularly have to be considered.

First, the weather was reasonably calm for February at the time the accident occurred. At that time, when remedies might have been available which would work in calm water, it was necessary to spend the time deciding exactly what should be done. I do not think it is unreasonable to suggest that the government and the Minister of Transport (Mr. Jamieson) in particular have a duty to have plans available for emergencies such as this. They have been developed elsewhere in the world in great abundance. Why did Canada not have a plan? Instead, we were faced with rather ridiculous experimentation. I say "ridiculous" because it should have been known exactly how to ignite fuel such as is aboard the Arrow. When the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Stanfield) made his point about planning, I thought it was a very sensible suggestion.

I am not at all sure any regulation would have, in fact, changed the situation.
I suggest there are a couple of regulations which could have, in fact, helped to avoid the Arrow disaster. There could be a requirement


that ships such as the Arrow use certain shipping lanes. I also suggest that they have Canadian pilots on board so that captains and crews could not sneak along a coastline with which they are not familiar, short-cutting, when they are carrying a lethal load.

Mr. Speaker, I am sorry that the Minister of Transport (Mr. Jamieson) is not here tonight, but I wish to inform my hon. friend that according to my information the minister is leaving almost immediately for Halifax, Nova Scotia, to make a personal inspection of the scene and to conduct his own inquiry into how the accident happened.
I also undertake to bring to his attention the suggestion made by the hon. member in regard to navigational safety. I wish to inform the hon. member that while the policy of providing adequate navigational aids for the conditions which prevail along our coast is not being re-examined at this time, the effectiveness of navigational aids in all ports is under continuous review. Where changes in traffic or other conditions dictate the need, aids as required will be provided.

NATIONAL FILM BOARD-RECONSIDERATION OF ORDER LEVYING CHARGES FOR USE OF FILMS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I congratulate the

hon. member for the interest he has shown in the NFB, a very important Canadian institution. I am sorry that I cannot add much to the answer given yesterday by the Secretary of State (Mr. Pelletier) during the question period. It is of interest to note what Mr. Saumier had to say on the matter in his recent report, and I quote:
The self-financing experience carried out with regard to the film-library appears worthwhile; an analysis of the results of this experience will show whether it is possible to make this field of activity more self-sustaining.
However, the Secretary of State said yesterday that if new factors had to be taken into account, this decision of the NFB might be amended.
I thank the hon. member for his comments and his useful suggestions which will be taken into serious consideration.

The National Conference on Price Stability, called by the Prices and Incomes Commission, met in Ottawa on February 9 and 10. It was attended by senior officers of national business and farm associations, representatives of professional groups, leaders of a broad spectrum of the Canadian business community and observers from the federal and provincial governments.
The Canadian business community had previously demonstrated its willingness to exercise a meaningful degree of restraint in pricing policies in 1970 through proposals made to the Commission by the Canadian Chambre of Commerce, the Canadian Manufacturers' Association, the Retail Council of Canada and the Canadian Bankers' Association.
While the groups represented at the Conference are prepared to take an initiative as a contribution to a broad program of restraint, they emphasize that an indispensable requirement for the control of inflation is a comparable measure of restraint by wage and salary earners, by governments at all levels and indeed by everyone.
There was broad agreement among those attending the Conference on the following:
(a)	Business firms generally, if called upon to do so, would reduce the number and size of price increases they would normally make in 1970.
(b)	More specifically, where higher prices are needed to cover higher costs, and market conditions made them feasible, business firms generally, if called upon to do so, would ensure that price increases were clearly less than the amount needed to cover the increases in costs at a normal volume of output and sales.
(c)	The Conference recognizes that domestic price criteria should not be applied to goods sold mainly in export markets. The Commission will keep the position of export industries under review and if it finds that developments in some of these industries are impairing the general price restraint program, it will seek appropriate solutions to the problems.
(d)	Business firms would be prepared to co-operate with the Prices and Incomes Commission in such price reviews as it might
decide to conduct (a brief outline of the proposed review procedure is appended).
(e)	The Conference recognizes that over most of agricultural production farmers do not have any significant discretion over the level of prices they receive. The representatives of agriculture present agreed that in the narrow range where the marketing system permits some price discretion, farmers, if called upon to do so, would act during 1970 in accordance with the general pricing criteria and procedures.
(f)	Specific commitments have already been given by the chartered banks for 1970 not to increase their existing schedule of service charges in Canada. They have also undertaken not to increase interest rates charged on Canadian dollar loans in Canada, except to the extent of any corresponding percentage point increase in the rates payable on Canadian dollar personal savings deposits. Trust and mortgage loan companies have agreed not to increase the existing spread between their prime mortgage lending rates and the highest rates paid on their term borrowings, and to refrain from increasing existing service charges on savings accounts. Representatives of life insurance companies, credit unions and other types of financial business affirmed their full support for the Commission's restraint program, and agreed that the principle that price increases should be held within cost increases should apply in their own operations.
(g)	That professional groups would be prepared to participate in a broad program of price restraint and to recommend to the provincial associations that they postpone or limit increases in existing fee schedules for professional services during 1970.
(h)	Representatives of the transportation, telecommunications and utilities industries endorsed the Commission's general criteria for price restraint. As a positive expression of co-operation, the members agreed to provide the Commission with thirty days' notice of any intent to increase general rate schedules.
(i)	The general merchandise sector of the retail and wholesale trades in determining pricing policies during 1970 would undertake not to increase initial markups on its various merchandise categories unless realized profit per dollar of sales would fall below that of

In such cases increases in markups would be sufficient only to restore returns to the level of the base period.
(k)	It is recognized that costs have been advancing particularly rapidly in most sectors of the construction industry and that special steps are needed by all concerned to reduce the rate of increase in these costs, including efforts to level out the flow of construction work. The representatives of the construction industry agreed that individual firms in the industry if called upon to do so would during 1970 absorb a proportion of their increased costs in accordance with the general pricing criteria.
Outline of Proposed Review Procedure
The price reviews are intended to ensure that the revenues produced by a price increase are less than the increases in costs that led to the price change, unless the increase in price is needed to improve a demonstrably inadequate rate of return on capital investment. Reviews will not be broad studies but will concentrate solely on compliance with the proposed pricing criteria.
The Commission is to be informed as soon as possible about any major price changes, but approval by the Commission in advance of the change in price is not necessary, and would not in general be practicable. The reviews will be conducted by a qualified staff of senior government officials and business executives who will be working with the Commission on a temporary basis.
Information needed to determine relevant revenue and cost changes will be requested by the price revie w staff in private meetings with the firm or firms involved. Actual operating records will be requested in most cases. Assistance in analysing data will be sought from fu ms but any conclusions reached will be made by the Commission as an independent body.
One of the main reasons for conducting price reviews on a detailed basis is to sort out cost changes arising from a change in the volume of sales from those due to a change in the price of inputs. The year 1969, or the nearest fiscal year, will in general be used as the base year when considering changes in costs and revenues. In cases where this would be clearly inappropriate, a suitable alternative base period would be selected.
During 1970 some firms may well experience unit cost increases as a result of a temporary decline in their volume of sales or output because of adverse market conditions. Such cost increases cannot be regarded as automatic justification for an equivalent price increase. On the other hand, some firms will experience unit cost decreases as a result of increases either in the volume of sales or in efficiency. In these cases, firms are expected to pass on some of the cost savings in terms of lower prices. The price review teams will attempt to decide what is reasonable price behavior in response to unit cost changes brought about by changes in volume. Consideration will be given to both the size and the likely duration of the "abnormal" sales volume.
Because of the care with which the price reviews must be made, it is proposed to concentrate them on important price increases by major firms and by market leaders in smaller markets. Some additional reviews may also be undertaken of less important price increases reported to the Commission by customers or other interested parties.
